Net fees: critic raised a concrete objection: The -13.17% YoY you apply is not consistent with the inputs you cite. Using your own figures and weights (FY2024→FY2025 -12.7% at 0.62 and FY2023→FY2024 -14.0% at 0.37) gives a weighted change of -13.054% (-12.7×0.62 + -14.0×0.37), not -13.17%. On that basis, multiplying 972.4 by (1−13.054%) would yield about £845.5m, so 844.357 is arithmetically inconsistent with your stated method and is biased low.
Pre-exceptional basic EPS: critic raised a concrete objection: You built FY2026 pre-exceptional EPS off a P&L that subtracts a £13.4m “net finance” charge and applies a 35.1% tax rate, but those look like statutory FY2025 figures, not the pre-exceptional finance cost and effective tax rate used for pre-exceptional EPS. This choice collapses the FY2026 EPS to 1.318p and, tellingly, back-solves FY2025 to an implied pre-exceptional operating profit of ~£45.5m (1.31p × 1,590.2m / (1−35.1%) + £13.4m), which can be checked against Hays’ FY2025 pre-exceptional operating profit and should be well lower given EPS fell 67% YoY (4.03p to 1.31p). In short, the EPS bridge is on the wrong basis: you used statutory net finance and tax instead of the pre-exceptional equivalents, making the FY2026 EPS too low.
